formality: Formal register ("Lei") for any sentence addressing the user directly — error messages, help text, emails (e.g. "Lei", never "tu"). Button and menu-action labels use the Italian imperative 2nd-person-singular form ("Applica", "Monta", "Archivia", "Smantella"), which is formality-neutral and is the standard convention in Italian desktop/web software (Microsoft/Adobe style), so it does not conflict with the Lei register used elsewhere.
styleNotes: 1) Keep hashcat/scheduler jargon in English when that is what Italian pentesters already use in writing (wordlist, mask, charset, chunk, keyspace, benchmark, hash rate, dashboard, potfile) — do not force an unfamiliar literal translation for an audience of security professionals. 2) Action buttons use the Italian imperative ("Applica", "Monta", "Archivia", "Svuota", "Smantella"); the corresponding noun forms ("archivio", "montaggio", "svuotamento", "smantellamento") are for status/section labels, not buttons. 3) Never use 'decifrare' (decrypt) for 'crack' — hashcat hashes are one-way and are not decrypted, so cracking must use 'craccare'/'craccato' (recovering the plaintext), not decryption vocabulary. 4) Match adjective gender/number to the Italian noun, not the English one (e.g. masculine 'tipo di hash', 'keyspace effettivo'; feminine 'soglia', 'condivisione di rete') — each term's note records the agreement to apply consistently across the UI.

hash.note: Technical term kept in Italian security and HashCat documentation

hashlist.note: Product concept, kept as KrakenHashes product term

hash type.note: Masculine: il tipo di hash (the hashcat hash mode, e.g. NTLM/mode 1000) — 'tipo' is masculine, so modifying adjectives agree masculine, not feminine.

crack.note: Standard Italian security-community verb for recovering a hash's plaintext. Do NOT use 'decifrare' (= decrypt): hashcat hashes are one-way functions and are never decrypted, only guessed/recovered, so decryption vocabulary is technically wrong here. 'Recuperare la password' is an acceptable paraphrase.

cracked.note: Agrees with noun gender: m. craccato, f. craccata; plural: craccati/craccate. Pairs with the verb 'craccare' (see 'crack'); avoid 'decifrato' for the same one-way-hash reason.

cracked hashes.note: Plural masculine ('hash' is invariable and treated as masculine); 'password craccate' if the context means the recovered passwords rather than the hash objects.

plaintext.note: Used in Italian cryptography literature; singular/plural same form

client potfile.note: 'cliente' = customer/engagement here (see 'client'), not a network client; 'del cliente' is more natural Italian than stacking the two nouns as 'potfile client'.

wordlist.note: Standard term in Italian HashCat documentation

rule.note: Standard Italian term for HashCat rule

rule file.note: Feminine plural: regole; also 'file regole' acceptable

mask.note: HashCat technical term, used unchanged in Italian documentation

charset.note: Technical term from HashCat; 'set di caratteri' is the translation but charset is standard

attack mode.note: Standard Italian terminology for attack modes

brute force.note: Also 'forza bruta' alone in casual UI; full form preferred for clarity

dictionary attack.note: Preferred form (preposition 'a'), matching 'attacco a forza bruta' for style consistency; the shorter 'attacco dizionario' is an acceptable colloquial variant.

association attack.note: HashCat mode 9; associativo agrees with attacco (masculine)

keyspace.note: Technical term from HashCat scheduling and benchmarking

chunk.note: KrakenHashes scheduler term; 'segmento' is translation but chunk is standard

task.note: Job execution terminology; 'attività' is acceptable translation

job.note: Core KrakenHashes term; 'lavoro' or 'processo' are translations

loopback.note: KrakenHashes attack continuation feature; ciclo di retroazione is translation

priority.note: Standard Italian term; feminine singular/plural same form

max agents.note: Plural masculine; or 'massimo di agenti' as alternative

overflow.note: KrakenHashes scheduler technical term; 'eccesso' is translation but overflow standard

benchmark.note: HashCat term; 'prova di velocità' or 'misurazione' are translations

hash rate.note: Standard in Italian HashCat output; also '(H/s)' in UI; 'velocità di hash' is translation

progress.note: Standard Italian software term for percent-complete (e.g. 'barra di avanzamento', 'stato di avanzamento'); 'progresso' is understood but reads as general advancement rather than a job's completion state.

device.note: Standard for GPU/CPU; also 'device' acceptable in technical context

claim code.note: Aligned with 'voucher' below since terms.json defines them as the same concept (the code used to register an agent) — using the same wording for both avoids presenting users with two different terms for one feature.

voucher.note: Registration credential; 'voucher' is standard in Italian business Italian

heartbeat.note: Agent communication term; 'battito cardiaco' or 'segnale di vita' are translations

offline buffer.note: Conveys the real meaning (grace period before an agent is marked offline) better than literal 'buffer offline', which reads as a memory/data buffer rather than a time window.

auto-update.note: Standard Italian UI term; also 'auto-aggiornamento' acceptable

binary.note: Masculine singular; refers to HashCat binary version

client.note: Refers to the customer/engagement the hashlists belong to (pentest-report sense), not a network client — Italian pentest reports standardly call this 'il cliente'. Keeping 'client' in English risks confusion with client-server terminology.

team.note: User group feature; 'team' or 'gruppo' are options

member.note: Masculine singular; 'i membri' plural; also 'utente' (user) acceptable

archive.note: Imperative button label (2nd person singular), matching the 'apply'→'applica' convention for action buttons; infinitive 'archiviare', noun 'archivio' for the archived-items area/section label.

password reuse.note: Masculine singular. Do not use 'password condivisa' (= a password shared between people) as an alternative — that is a different scenario from the same password recurring across several accounts.

complexity.note: Feminine singular/plural same form; password attribute

domain.note: Masculine singular; Windows/AD context; 'do not translate' list includes Active Directory

username.note: Masculine singular; standard UI term in Italian

audit log.note: Masculine singular; 'log di audit' or 'registro di controllo' acceptable

dashboard.note: Standard term; 'pannello' or 'pannello di controllo' are translations

settings.note: Feminine plural; standard Italian UI term

apply.note: Imperative button label (2nd person singular); infinitive: 'applicare'

SAN.note: Abbreviation universally kept in Italian certificate/TLS documentation (it is not actually itself listed in terms.json's doNotTranslate array, but it follows the same logic as SSL/TLS/DNS there). The literal translation 'Nome alternativo del soggetto' is never used in practice.

mount.note: Imperative button label for the mount action, matching 'apply'→'applica'; infinitive 'montare', noun 'montaggio' (cf. 'punto di montaggio' = mount point) for status/section labels.

provisioning.note: Cloud infrastructure term; 'provisioning' is standard; 'allocazione' translation available

budget.note: Cloud spending context; 'budget' adopted in Italian business; 'bilancio' is translation

drain.note: Imperative button label matching 'apply'→'applica'; infinitive 'svuotare', noun 'svuotamento' for a status label (e.g. 'In svuotamento'). Allow-finish-no-new-work semantic, not literal emptying.

teardown.note: Imperative button label matching 'apply'→'applica' (cloud instance destruction); infinitive 'smantellare', noun 'smantellamento' (or 'dismissione') for a status/log label.

webhook.note: HTTP callback term; kept in Italian technical documentation

two-factor authentication.note: Feminine singular; also MFA or 2FA abbreviations used

authenticator app.note: Describes the generic class of TOTP app; more natural Italian than anglicized 'app authenticator'. Users will still recognize specific apps (Google/Microsoft Authenticator) by their own product names.

API key.note: Feminine singular; personal HTTP API authentication
